title: Society and manners
note: Rome's patricians were the old ruling families and its plebeians the common citizens; both words still mark class. Hoi polloi, Greek for the many, means the common people, not the elite, though it is often misused. Gauche, French for left, means socially awkward, and a faux pas, a false step, is a social blunder.

read.title: The Dinner Party
text: Marguerite Vance had hosted the same dinner every December for thirty years, and her guests knew its mores by heart: no talk of money, no phones at the table, and no leaving before the cheese.

This year she invited a newcomer. Leo Brandt had made a fortune in frozen pizza and bought the old Ashby house on the hill. A few guests whispered that he was a parvenu. Others, less patrician themselves, simply wondered whether he would know which fork to use.

He did not. He reached for the dessert spoon during the soup, asked the bishop what his house had cost, and laughed loudly at his own jokes. It was one faux pas after another, and the table's hauteur grew colder by the course.

Then the power went out. In the dark, the guests discovered that Brandt was a superb raconteur. He told of selling pizzas from a borrowed van, of nearly going broke twice, and of the night a health inspector became his first investor. His bonhomie warmed the room more than the candles did.

By the time the lights returned, the evening had become the most convivial in years. Marguerite noticed that the guests who had been ready to ostracize him were now asking for his number. Good manners, she decided, could be learned; savoir-faire of the heart was rarer.

q.q: Why did some guests call Brandt a parvenu?
o: He came from an old noble family

q.q: What changed the guests' opinion of him?
o: His skill at telling stories during the blackout

q.q: "The table's hauteur grew colder" means the guests became
